one_liner: Small header-only C++23 coroutine runtime for Linux: per-thread epoll loops with SO_REUSEPORT, ~1.13x Tokio req/s on one loopback test.
what_it_does: Rain is a Linux-only async runtime made of a lazy coroutine Task<T>, one EventLoop per worker thread (epoll reactor, 1 ms four-level timer wheel, signalfd), TcpListener/TcpStream awaiters with timeout and sendfile variants, and a ThreadPool + eventfd bridge behind spawn_blocking(). You build a Runtime with N workers and pass a setup callback that runs once per loop, usually to bind that loop's own listener and spawn an accept loop; EventLoop::submit() moves work to another loop explicitly. Failures come back as Result<T, E> (std::expected), not exceptions. The API borrows Tokio's shape but is C++, so it is not a drop-in for Tokio or Asio.
how_it_is_fast: It is thread-per-core and shared-nothing: each loop binds its own SO_REUSEPORT listener (on by default), the kernel spreads incoming connections across them, and a task stays on the loop that accepted it, so there is no work-stealing and no cross-thread wakeup on the hot path. The reactor tries read()/write()/accept4() before suspending. Waiters are registered edge-triggered with EPOLLONESHOT in a vector indexed by fd instead of a hash map, so every blocked wait costs one epoll_ctl re-arm. The README attributes the gap over Tokio to skipping work-stealing and relying on kernel SO_REUSEPORT balancing.
when_to_use: Linux servers with many similar, short request/response connections (HTTP keep-alive, small RPCs) where SO_REUSEPORT's kernel distribution keeps the loops evenly loaded
C++23 codebases that want coroutine networking from a small header-only runtime they can read end to end and vendor
Targets that stay on plain epoll because io_uring is unavailable or not wanted
Designs that want explicit placement (EventLoop::submit to a chosen loop) instead of a scheduler that migrates tasks on its own
when_not_to_use: Non-Linux targets: epoll, eventfd and signalfd are hard requirements
Skewed load (a few heavy connections or CPU-bound handlers): with no work-stealing, a busy connection monopolises its loop while other cores sit idle

Very high connection counts: every loop iteration runs std::erase_if over all live tasks, then takes a mutex and does an eventfd read() to drain the cross-core queue. The only published run used 256 connections

Stacks that need TLS, HTTP parsing, UDP or an ecosystem. net/ has TCP only, and fs/ is file I/O on the blocking pool, whose queue is a mutex + condvar Channel that the code itself calls architecture debt

Maturity-sensitive code: single author, no releases. Use-after-free bugs in block_on and in when_all/when_any, lost cross-core submits, and a timer cascade bug that fired timers a full wheel-lap late were fixed only in June 2026

integration.dependencies: none beyond pthreads and Linux headers (CMake INTERFACE target rain_core; there are no install/export rules, so use add_subdirectory or add src/ to the include path)
integration.min_toolchain: C++23 with std::expected. The README says GCC 13+ or Clang 17+ and CMake 3.28+. CI builds with g++-14 and clang++-19, because the repo's CI notes say Clang 18 with libstdc++ 14 hides std::expected
integration.platforms: Linux only (epoll, eventfd, signalfd); no architecture-specific code seen; CI runs on GitHub's ubuntu-24.04 runner
integration.thread_safety: Each EventLoop, with its reactor and timer, is single-threaded. EventLoop::submit(), request_stop() and request_graceful_stop() may be called from any thread (mutex + eventfd wakeup). Task cancellation runs stop_callbacks on the calling thread and touches the reactor, so task.hpp says callers must not request a task's stop from another core

gotchas: ListenOptions defaults to reuse_port=true and backlog=128. A second copy of the server on the same port binds silently and splits the connections; the author's perf_matrix.sh warns about this 'silent stacking'. The benchmark raises backlog to 4096
Executor::run() sets SIGPIPE to SIG_IGN for the whole process. Worker threads are not pinned to CPUs despite the 'per-core' naming, so use taskset or your own affinity code, as perf_matrix.sh does

co_await on a Task<T> whose T is not a Result is undefined behavior if the task was cancelled (task.hpp says so). unhandled_exception() replaces any exception with a generic 'unhandled exception' error and loses the original
The timer wheel ticks at 1 ms and documents a maximum delay of about 18.6 h, but schedule_at() neither clamps nor rejects longer delays, and the behavior for them is not documented
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick Rain for a small, readable C++23 thread-per-core coroutine runtime on plain epoll; if io_uring is allowed, Condy (header-only C++20 over io_uring) or uring_exec are the C++ options. If the goal is beating Tokio, monoio (~1.9x Tokio peak echo QPS on 4 cores) and ringline carry much stronger evidence, and ringline's own 2x2 shows a per-core Tokio closes most of the gap, which suggests Rain's win over default Tokio is mostly a scheduler-configuration effect.
verified_claims_summary: In one first-party loopback run on an AMD Ryzen 5 5600H (6C/12T), with wrk -t4 -c256 -d15s on the same host, Rain (4 SO_REUSEPORT loops, CMake Release, C++ compiler and version not stated) served a canned 'Hello, World!' HTTP/1.1 response at 247,283 req/s (max latency 9.31 ms) against 219,543 req/s (18.45 ms) for a default #[tokio::main] server built with cargo --release, LTO and codegen-units=1. The repo's own perf_matrix.sh says that default Tokio ran 12 workers to Rain's hard-coded 4, unpinned and without warmup, and its pinned thread-parity scenario has no published results; the README table was last edited 2026-04-29, before the June 2026 reactor and timer rewrites.
status_note: Single-author and MIT-licensed, small enough to vendor; last commit 2026-06-25 (about three months ago) with no tags, releases or outside issues, though CI runs the tests under ASan/UBSan and TSan plus a libFuzzer job and a nightly TSan soak.
